book.title: Coercive Control: How Men Entrap Women in Personal Life

argument.statement: Coercive control—abuse combining isolation, intimidation, and control, sometimes without physical attacks—is the more prevalent and devastating domestic abuse and should have legal standing as a defense for women who attack or kill abusers.

book.rationale: The book primarily addresses the dynamics of coercive control in relationships, focusing on gendered experiences of domestic abuse, while also engaging with broader societal implications.
book.summary: The battle against domestic violence has focused primarily on incidents of extreme physical abuse and the resulting trauma to the victim. While there is a growing understanding of some forms of psychological abuse, such as stalking, there is less understanding of the pattern of abuse where physical attacks are combined with isolation, intimidation, and control. Stark argues that "coercive control"-which may not include any physical abuse-is actually the more prevalent and devastating form of domestic abuse, yet remains largely invisible to the helping professionals and has no legal standing. He contends that interventions are ineffective for a large number of battered women due to the gap between what these women experience and the singular emphasis on male violence and victim trauma. Drawing extensively on cases, Stark identifies the problems with our current approach to domestic violence, outlines the components of coercive control, and then uses this alternate framework to analyze the cases of battered women charged with criminal offenses directed at their abusers. He presents the controversial notion that "coercive control" should be a legal defense for women who attack or kill their abusers.
